summary:
San Juan is a province of Argentina and stands under the country's national legal framework. No source records a San Juan-specific departure from that framework on gender recognition, document markers or entry rules, so the province is assessed at the national position.

Argentina's Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, remains formally in force. It permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and Argentine identity documents have carried an "X" marker since 2021. Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, and the United Nations described the 2012 statute as a pioneering regional step for transgender rights.

The framework has been narrowed by executive decree rather than by repeal of the statute. Decree 62/2025, published on 5 February 2025 under President Javier Milei, amended Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to bar people under 18 from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions. Decree 61/2025 amended sentencing law to change the placement of transgender detainees. Both apply nationally and reach every province, San Juan included.

Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations called both decrees unconstitutional and warned that abruptly suspending adolescent treatment endangers trans youth, and they filed a judicial challenge to them. Until a court rules, the decrees govern, and transgender visitors who are under 18 should expect the surgical and hormonal prohibitions to apply to them here as anywhere else in Argentina.

Trans activists interviewed in Buenos Aires in April 2025 described the situation facing their community as chaotic and desperate. They reported that the national government eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed transgender hires made under a federal quota reserving 1% of public-sector posts, which they said is no longer being implemented. The same activists said the 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026 and described them as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments for Argentina on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, an assessment of deterioration that sits alongside a statute still formally among the most permissive in the region. The same overview's basis for the gender-recognition rating is not set out in the sources available here.

Conditions reported by activists in Buenos Aires serve as an illustration of the national picture rather than as evidence about San Juan specifically. Two of the organisations whose spokespeople spoke to the press in April 2025 are named for trans people killed in Argentina, Diana Sacayán in 2015 and Lohana Berkins, which is why their testimony carries weight on the durability of the 2012 statute.

Argentina's position is split between a permissive statute and a narrowing practice: the 2012 law, the 2010 marriage equality statute and the United Nations' description of the gender identity law as pioneering describe the formal framework, while the 2025 decrees, the elimination of the dedicated ministry and the 2025 hate-crime record describe what is enforced.
localsOnly:
The federal Trans Labor Quota Law reserves 1% of public-sector posts for transgender workers. Activists said in April 2025 that the national government dismissed trans hires made under the quota and that the law is no longer being implemented, which bears on resident employment rather than on visitors.

Decree 61/2025 changes where transgender detainees are held under sentencing law. Its practical effect falls on residents in the prison system; legal experts and LGBT+ organisations called the decree unconstitutional and it faces judicial challenge.

Decree 62/2025 bars under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions, affecting trans minors resident in Argentina and their families. Legal experts said abruptly suspending adolescent treatments endangers trans youth.

Anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial law in Argentina, and hate-crime recording is carried out by the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio, whose 2025 figures were published by Agencia Presentes on 19 March 2026. Whether San Juan maintains its own reporting channel or provincial anti-discrimination procedure is not addressed in the sources available here.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the judicial challenge to decrees 62/2025 and 61/2025 is not recorded in the sources available here; whether the decrees have been upheld, stayed or struck down remains unresolved.

No source in the record addresses San Juan's own implementing procedure, its provincial courts, or enforcement of Law 26.743 by San Juan authorities. Whether the province has issued any guidance on document markers, detention placement or adolescent care is unresolved rather than confirmed as absent.

No San Juan-level data on hate crimes, violence against trans people or discrimination complaints appears in the record; the 227 recorded hate crimes for 2025 are national figures.

Whether the reported non-implementation of the 1% trans employment quota has been litigated, and whether any reinstatement of dismissed workers has been ordered, is not sourced here.
